endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Govern agentic memory: if the agent maintains persistent memory across sessions, that memory store must be brought under formal data governance (access controls, retention policies, BAA coverage).

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Verify GAI system training data and TEVV data provenance, and that fine-tuning or retrieval-augmented generation data is grounded.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Evaluate whether data inputs and provenance enable accuracy, ensure completeness, and facilitate the management of bias in datasets [3], [4].

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations and Fundamental Principles of Large Language Models in Medical Education: Viewpoint
endorsements.quote: Develop independent LLM databases: all training data should be reviewed by clinical experts before incorporation to ensure authenticity and accuracy.

endorsements.title: Beyond Pattern Recognition: Call for Functionally Aware AI for Anatomical Illustration
endorsements.quote: The most promising solution lies in developing highly specialized “expert AIs” trained not on the chaotic internet, but on meticulously curated, gold standard datasets.

evidence.title: Representation Before Retrieval: Structured Patient Artifacts Reduce Hallucination in Clinical AI Systems
evidence.outcome: unsupported claim rate with structured artifacts
evidence.effect: Unsupported claims were 8.4% (95% CI: 6.7–10.3%), reported as 40% relative reduction versus baseline; p = 0.02; d = 0.48.
evidence.quote: Structured artifacts reduced unsupported claims to 8.4% (95% CI: 6.7–10.3%) in single-pass generation, a 40% relative reduction versus baseline (  p = 0.02,  d = 0.48).
evidence.sample_unit: generated outputs (100 synthetic vignettes x 3 seeds x 4 conditions)

evidence.title: EyeRAG: graph retrieval-augmented generation for safe and accurate clinical dialogue in ophthalmology
evidence.effect: Audit of 200 entities and 200 relationships found 100% guideline-presence precision and 100% description accuracy.
evidence.quote: The audit yielded 100% precision for guideline presence and 100% accuracy for descriptions, with no errors detected.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical scenarios (270 internal questions plus 30 external questions)

evidence.title: AI-generated data contamination erodes pathological variability and diagnostic reliability
evidence.effect: More than 800,000 synthetic data points showed rapid erosion of pathological variability and diagnostic reliability.
evidence.quote: Here, we show that in the absence of mandatory human verification, this self-referential cycle drives a rapid erosion of pathological variability and diagnostic reliability of medical data at population scale.

commentary.bottom_line: Two offline vignette studies suggest that documenting data provenance and auditing retrieval sources may reduce unsupported model claims, but neither study measured patient outcomes or tested expert review of clinical fine-tuning pairs. The recommendation rests mainly on framework endorsements, with very low certainty that the practice improves care.

perspectives.view: One simulation reported unsupported claims at 8.4% (95% CI 6.7–10.3%) with structured artifacts, a 40% relative reduction versus baseline (p = 0.02). A second audited 200 entities and 200 relationships and found 100% guideline-presence precision. Both are single, offline studies of synthetic or scripted cases, so indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

A benchmark of more than 800,000 synthetic data points showed erosion of pathological variability and diagnostic reliability, which shows the contamination hazard exists. It does not show that provenance checks prevent it. The 8.4% residual unsupported claim rate suggests documentation may reduce, but does not remove, errors that could reach clinicians.

The knowledge-graph audit suggests retrieval sources can be checked against guidelines at the entity and relationship level. The study did not report reviewer hours, expert staffing, or how often audits must repeat as guidelines change, so the burden of sustaining this in production remains unknown.

One study was conducted in China and the other did not report a setting, and both used synthetic or scripted scenarios. Neither examined whether curated or audited data represent Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so provenance review could certify data that still underrepresent these groups.

NIST AI 600-1 and the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide advise verifying training, fine-tuning, and retrieval data provenance. The CHAI playbook states that persistent agent memory must fall under data governance, including BAA coverage. No supplied study tests documentation formats or compliance with these provisions.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployed models built with and without documented data lineage or expert-reviewed fine-tuning pairs in live clinical use, and none reports reviewer workload, cost, or effects on patient-level errors.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; both used synthetic or scripted cases. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that provenance review improves output fidelity for their patients.
